introduction.p: A parametric curve is described by coordinate functions x(t) and y(t) on a specified parameter interval. The parameter may represent time, but it need not. The description records how the curve is traced, including its direction and possible repeated traversal.

subsection.p: The curve itself is the circle. The parametrization tells more: it tells where the point is at each time, the direction of travel, and how fast the point moves.
This extra information is often useful. A road map shows the road. A schedule tells how the traveler moves along it. A parametric curve contains both.

note.title: Parametrization of a plane curve
note.p: A parametrization of a plane curve is a pair of functions
defined for t in an interval I. The moving point
traces the curve as t runs through I.
The variable t is called a parameter. It is often time, but it does not have to be.

exercise.title: What extra information does a parametrization carry?

statement.p: The unit circle can be drawn as the set x^2+y^2=1, or traced by (\cos t,\sin t). In your own words, what does the moving-point description add that the Cartesian equation does not, and why is that extra information often useful?

hint.p: A road map shows the road. A schedule tells where the traveler is, in what order, and how fast. A parametrization contains both.

example.p: Since y=t, we can substitute directly:
This is a parabola opening to the right. It is not the graph of a single function y=f(x), because most x-values to the right of -1 have two y-values.
The parametric form has no trouble with this. It gives exactly one point for each value of t:

exercise.title: What does eliminating the parameter forget?

statement.p: Three different parametrizations can satisfy the same equation x^2+y^2=1 while tracing the circle once, twice, or clockwise. In your own words, what information is lost in the Cartesian equation, and why can ignoring the parameter interval accidentally enlarge the curve?

hint.p: Elimination remembers the set of points, not orientation, speed, starting point, ending point, or repeated tracing. The domain of t is part of the description.

warning.title: Warning
warning.p: A Cartesian equation describes the set of points on the curve. A parametrization also describes the motion along the curve.
When you eliminate the parameter, you may lose:

p.em: orientation, speed, starting point, ending point, repeated tracing.

subsection.p: There is another warning. Eliminating the parameter can accidentally enlarge the curve if the parameter interval is ignored.

note.title: Parametrization as schedule
note.p: A geometric curve tells where the point can be.
A parametrization tells where the point is, in what order, and at what rate.

paragraphs.p: This distinction will matter when we compute slopes, lengths, and areas. The geometry may be unchanged, but the parameter controls the calculations.

exercise.title: Why can the same geometric curve have many parametrizations?

statement.p: A line segment from A to B can be traced at constant speed, from rest, or backward. In your own words, why is that not a nuisance, and what distinction does the phrase parametrization as schedule capture?

hint.p: The geometric curve tells where the point can be. The parametrization tells where it is, in what order, and at what rate.

exercise.title: Why does zero speed not always mean the curve ends?

statement.p: Speed along a parametric curve is \sqrt{(x')^2+(y')^2}. In your own words, why can that speed be zero at an interior time, and why is such a pause a feature of the schedule rather than necessarily a feature of the geometric curve?

hint.p: A traveler can stop on an otherwise ordinary road. The curve may continue; the chosen parametrization may simply rest for an instant.

example.title: a point that pauses
example.p: The curve is the x-axis. The point moves along it, passing through the origin at t=0. Its speed is
At t=0, the speed is 0. The point momentarily stops, then continues moving to the right.
A zero speed does not always mean the curve ends. It may only mean the chosen schedule has a pause.
The next section asks how to do calculus on such curves. A tangent slope is no longer found from y=f(x). Instead, both x and y are changing, and the slope must be built from their rates.
